My cousin **is staying** with us this month.
We**'re learning** about volcanoes in class this week.
Ben **is learning** Japanese this year.
How **is** your new job **going**?

mistakes.wrong: I read a really good book at the moment.
mistakes.right: I'm reading a really good book at the moment.

mistakes.wrong: My sister stays with us this month.
mistakes.right: My sister is staying with us this month.

points.title: Future arrangements: I'm meeting Sam tonight
points.summary: Use the present continuous for future plans that are already arranged, usually with a time.

blocks.md: Use the present continuous for **future arrangements**: plans you've already made, often with a time, a place or other people: *I**'m meeting** Sam at 6 tonight. We**'re flying** to Rome on Monday.*
Common words: *tonight, tomorrow, on Friday, next week, at the weekend.*
*Be going to* is also correct for plans: *I'm going to meet Sam at 6.* For timetables, use the present simple: *The film **starts** at 8.* See [Future Forms](/blog/grammar/future-forms/).

examples.text: I**'m meeting** Sam at 6 tonight.
We**'re flying** to Rome on Monday.
What **are** you **doing** this weekend?
She**'s starting** her new job next week.
They **aren't coming** to the party.

mistakes.wrong: I see the dentist tomorrow. (my appointment)
mistakes.right: I'm seeing the dentist tomorrow.

mistakes.wrong: What do you do this weekend?
mistakes.right: What are you doing this weekend?

points.title: Changing situations: It's getting colder
points.summary: Use the present continuous for situations that are changing now: get, become, increase, improve.

blocks.md: Use the present continuous for a **change that is happening** at the moment: *The weather **is getting** colder. Prices **are rising**.*
Verbs often used this way: *get, become, change, improve, increase, rise, fall, grow, start, begin.* *Get* + comparative is very common: *It's **getting darker**. Your English is **getting better**.*

examples.text: The weather **is getting** colder.
Prices **are rising** again.
Your English **is improving** fast.
The city **is growing** every year.
I**'m starting** to enjoy my new job.

mistakes.wrong: The population increases very fast at the moment.
mistakes.right: The population is increasing very fast at the moment.
mistakes.why: A change happening now: present continuous.

mistakes.wrong: It gets dark. Let's go home.
mistakes.right: It's getting dark. Let's go home.
mistakes.why: A change happening now: present continuous.

points.title: always + continuous: He's always complaining
points.summary: always / constantly / forever + continuous for something that happens too often, often annoying.

blocks.md: *Always, constantly* or *forever* + present continuous means something happens **very often, often too often**. We usually use it to complain: *He**'s always complaining**. You**'re forever losing** your keys!*
Compare: *I **always walk** to work* = every time, a normal habit (neutral).
Word order: **be + always + verb-ing**: *She**'s always interrupting** me.* (not *always is interrupting*)

examples.text: He**'s always complaining** about something.
You**'re always losing** your keys!
My neighbour **is constantly playing** loud music.
She**'s forever borrowing** my phone.
I **always walk** to work.

mistakes.wrong: She always is interrupting me.
mistakes.right: She's always interrupting me.

mistakes.wrong: I'm always going to work by bike. (my normal habit)
mistakes.right: I always go to work by bike.
mistakes.why: For a neutral habit, use the present simple.

points.title: In progress at a regular time; always for typical behaviour
points.summary: At 8 I'm usually driving = in the middle of it at that time; always + continuous can also describe typical (even positive) behaviour.

blocks.md: Use the present continuous for an action that is **in progress at a regular time**: *At 7 a.m. I**'m usually having** breakfast, so call me later.* Compare: *I usually **have** breakfast at 7* = that's when I start it.
*Always / constantly* + continuous describes **typical behaviour**. It's often a complaint, but it can also be positive: *My neighbour **is always bringing** us cakes. She's so kind.*

examples.text: At 7 a.m. I**'m usually having** breakfast.
Don't call between 6 and 7: we**'re usually eating** then.
On Saturday mornings I**'m normally working** in the garden.
She**'s always helping** other people.
Whenever I visit, he**'s watching** TV.

mistakes.wrong: At 8 I'm usually drive to work.
mistakes.right: At 8 I'm usually driving to work.

mistakes.wrong: She's always help people.
mistakes.right: She's always helping people.

points.title: When not to use it for the future
points.summary: Use the present continuous for arranged or decided plans, not for predictions or permanent future situations.

blocks.md: The present continuous for the future suggests something **arranged or firmly decided**: *I**'m not lending** him my car again.* So we don't use it for:

items: **Predictions** about things nobody can arrange, like the weather: *It**'s going to rain** tonight. / It**'ll rain** tonight.* (not *It's raining tonight*)
**Permanent** future situations: *People **will live** longer in the future.* (not *are living longer in the future*)

blocks.md: With **go** and **come**, many people prefer the present continuous to *going to go / going to come*: *I**'m going** to town on Saturday. **Are** you **coming** home for lunch?*

examples.text: I**'m going** to Toronto next week.
**Are** you **coming** home for lunch?
It**'s going to snow** tonight.
Experts say the population **will grow**.
I**'m not lending** him my car again.

mistakes.wrong: It's raining tomorrow.
mistakes.right: It's going to rain tomorrow. / It'll rain tomorrow.
mistakes.why: The weather can't be arranged: use going to or will.

mistakes.wrong: In the future, people are living on other planets.
mistakes.right: In the future, people will live on other planets.
mistakes.why: Predictions about the future: will or going to.

items.prompt: What does *At 7 I'm usually having breakfast* mean?
options: I usually start breakfast at exactly 7.
At 7 I'm usually in the middle of breakfast.
items.explanation: Continuous = the action is **in progress** at that time.

items.prompt: Which sentence describes kind, typical behaviour?
options: She's going to help her neighbours.
items.explanation: *Always* + continuous can describe typical behaviour, here positive.

items.prompt: Whenever I phone him, he ___.
items.explanation: In progress whenever I phone: *he's watching TV*.

items.prompt: Look at the forecast. It ___ tomorrow.
items.explanation: The weather can't be arranged: *it's going to snow*.

items.prompt: Which sentence is NOT correct?
options: In 2080, people will live on the Moon.
In 2080, people are living on the Moon.
I think people will live on the Moon one day.
Maybe people are going to live on the Moon.
items.explanation: A prediction about the future: use *will* or *going to*, not the present continuous.

items.prompt: Which sentence is a prediction, not an arrangement?
options: We're flying to Rome on Friday.
She's having a party on Saturday.
items.explanation: Nobody can arrange the sea level: it's a prediction (*will*).

topics.h1: Present Perfect Continuous (I have been doing)
topics.summary: An activity that started in the past and continues now, or has just stopped: I've been waiting for an hour.
intro: We use the **present perfect continuous** (*have / has been* + *-ing*) for an activity that started in the past and is **still going on**, or has **just stopped**: *I**'ve been waiting** for an hour. You're wet! **Have** you **been swimming**?*

It focuses on the **activity** and **how long** it has lasted. The present perfect simple (*I've done*) focuses on the **result** or **how much**. This page covers both and the cases where the choice changes the meaning.

points.title: Form and use: still going on, how long
points.summary: **have / has been + -ing** for an activity that started in the past and continues now, often with *how long, for, since*.

rows: *I**'ve been learning** English for three years.*

blocks.md: The activity started in the past and is **still happening**: *It**'s been raining** all day* (and it's still raining). *How long **have** you **been learning** to drive?*
Common time words: *for, since, how long, all day, all morning, recently, lately*.
*She's been* = *she has been*. Don't confuse *she's been working* (present perfect continuous) with *she's working* (present continuous, now).

examples.text: I**'ve been studying** for this exam for weeks.
How long **has** it **been snowing**?
They**'ve been building** that bridge since 2022.
We **haven't been sleeping** well recently.

mistakes.wrong: I'm waiting for an hour.
mistakes.right: I've been waiting for an hour.
mistakes.why: How long up to now: present perfect continuous.

mistakes.wrong: She has been work here since May.
mistakes.right: She has been working here since May.

mistakes.wrong: How long you have been learning English?
mistakes.right: How long have you been learning English?

points.title: An activity that has just stopped: evidence now
points.summary: We use it for an activity that has **recently stopped** when we can see the **result** now: *You're out of breath. Have you been running?*

blocks.md: The activity may have **just finished**, but we can see or feel its effects now:

items: *Your eyes are red. **Have** you **been crying**?*
*I'm tired because I**'ve been working** in the garden.*
*The ground is wet. It**'s been raining**.*

blocks.md: The focus is on the **activity** (what you have been doing), not on a completed result.
For something that is finished and its **completed** result, use the simple: *I**'ve washed** the car.* (It's clean.) *I**'ve been washing** the car.* (That's why I'm wet.)

examples.text: Sorry I'm dirty. I**'ve been fixing** the car.
The kitchen smells of onions. **Have** you **been cooking**?
Why are you so tired? ~ I**'ve been running**.

mistakes.wrong: Your eyes are red. Have you been cry?
mistakes.right: Your eyes are red. Have you been crying?

mistakes.wrong: My hands hurt because I've been dig in the garden.
mistakes.right: My hands hurt because I've been digging in the garden.

points.title: Have been doing or have done?
points.summary: **have been doing** = the activity, how long, maybe not finished. **have done** = completed, a result, how many / how much.

rows: *She**'s been writing** emails all morning.* (how long)
*They**'ve been painting** the kitchen.* (that's why it smells)

blocks.md: Ask **how long?** → usually continuous: *How long **have** you **been playing** tennis?* Ask **how many / how much?** → simple: *How many matches **have** you **played**?*

With **for / since**, the continuous is common for activities: *I've been learning Persian **for** two years.* With *live* and *work*, both are possible: *I**'ve lived / 've been living** here for ten years.*
Don't use the continuous with a number of completed things: *I've drunk three coffees.* Not *I've been drinking three coffees*.

examples.text: I**'ve been cooking** all afternoon.
I**'ve cooked** dinner. Come and eat!
He**'s been saving** money for a new car.
He**'s saved** $5,000 so far.

mistakes.wrong: I've been reading three books this month.
mistakes.right: I've read three books this month.

mistakes.wrong: Look! I've been finishing my homework.
mistakes.right: Look! I've finished my homework.

points.title: Repeated actions and temporary situations
points.summary: The continuous can describe **repeated** actions over a period (*I've been going to the gym a lot*) and **temporary** situations (*I've been staying with friends*).

blocks.md: The activity doesn't have to be continuous. It can be **repeated** many times up to now: *I**'ve been playing** a lot of tennis recently. She**'s been calling** me every day.*
It also suggests a **temporary** situation: *I**'ve been staying** at my sister's since I came back.* (not permanent) Compare: *I**'ve lived** here all my life.* (permanent)
With *always*, use the simple: *I**'ve always lived** in Kerman.* Not *I've always been living*.
A single short action in the continuous suggests repetition: *He**'s been kicking** the ball against the wall* (again and again). *He**'s kicked** the ball over the fence* (once).

examples.text: I**'ve been going** to bed late recently.
We**'ve been using** my brother's car while ours is being repaired.
The phone**'s been ringing** all morning.
My grandparents **have lived** in this village all their lives.

mistakes.wrong: I've always been living in Toronto.
mistakes.right: I've always lived in Toronto.

mistakes.wrong: She's been phoning me twice today.
mistakes.right: She's phoned me twice today.

points.title: State verbs and verbs with two meanings
points.summary: State verbs use the **simple**: *I've known her for years.* Verbs like *have, think, see* can be continuous only in their action meaning: *I've been thinking about it.*

blocks.md: Verbs for **states** (*know, believe, like, love, want, own, belong, understand, be*) are not normally used in the continuous, even with *for* or *since*: *I**'ve known** him since school.* Not *I've been knowing him*.
Some verbs have a **state** meaning and an **action** meaning:
For the full list of state verbs, see [Stative Verbs](/blog/grammar/stative-verbs/).

examples.text: We**'ve known** each other for twenty years.
I**'ve wanted** a dog since I was a child.
I**'ve been thinking** of changing jobs.
They**'ve been having** a lot of fun on holiday.

mistakes.wrong: I've been knowing her since 2015.
mistakes.right: I've known her since 2015.

mistakes.wrong: She's been owning that shop for years.
mistakes.right: She's owned that shop for years.

points.title: Subtle differences: temporary, unfinished, annoyed
points.summary: The continuous can make a situation sound **temporary**, **unfinished**, or **annoying**: *Who's been using my computer?* The simple sounds more **permanent** or **complete**.

blocks.md: When both forms are grammatical, the continuous adds a nuance:

items: **Temporary vs permanent**: *She**'s been working** in sales* (maybe for now) / *She**'s worked** in sales for twenty years* (her career).
**Unfinished vs complete**: *I**'ve been reading** the report* (I'm in the middle) / *I**'ve read** the report* (I can discuss it).
**Complaint or surprise**: *Who**'s been using** my laptop? Someone**'s been eating** my chocolate!* (I can see signs, and I'm annoyed.)
**Repeated intention**: *I**'ve been meaning** to call you.* (I intended to many times, but didn't.)

blocks.md: In negative sentences, the simple often focuses on the gap since the last time: *I **haven't slept** for two days* (not at all). The continuous describes a pattern: *I **haven't been sleeping** well* (badly, recently).

In formal writing and reports, the simple is preferred for completed achievements: *The project **has reduced** costs by 15%.* The continuous suits ongoing processes: *We **have been monitoring** the results.*

examples.text: Someone**'s been reading** my diary!
I**'ve been meaning** to tell you something.
I **haven't eaten** since breakfast.
I **haven't been eating** well lately.

mistakes.wrong: I've been meaning tell you.
mistakes.right: I've been meaning to tell you.

mistakes.wrong: The company has been reducing costs by 15% so far. (a completed result)
mistakes.right: The company has reduced costs by 15% so far.

items.prompt: You find your desk in a mess. You say: *Who ___ my things?*
items.explanation: Annoyance at evidence: present perfect continuous.

items.prompt: Which sentence describes a career, not a temporary job?
options: He's been working as a journalist this month.
He's worked as a journalist for thirty years.
He's working as a journalist for now.
He's been working at a café while he studies.
items.explanation: The simple + a long period sounds permanent.

items.prompt: I ___ (mean) to reply to your email for days. Sorry!
items.explanation: A repeated intention: *have been meaning to*.

topics.summary: I've lost my keys (connected to now) or I lost my keys yesterday (finished time).
intro: Both tenses talk about the past. The **past simple** (*I lost*) is about a **finished** time. The **present perfect** (*I've lost*) connects the past with **now**.
The most important question is: **do you say or mean a finished time?** If yes, use the past simple. This page goes from that basic rule to the cases where both are possible.

points.title: Finished time or up to now?
points.summary: Past simple with a **finished time** (*yesterday, last week, in 2019, ago*). Present perfect when there's **no finished time** and the past is connected to now.

headers: Present perfect (up to now / no time given)

blocks.md: Words with a **finished time** take the past simple: *yesterday, last night / week / year, ago, in 2015, on Monday, when I was a child, What time…? When…?*
Words that mean **up to now** often take the present perfect: *ever, never, already, yet, so far, since, for* (up to now).
You can't use the present perfect with a finished time: *I saw him yesterday.* Not *I've seen him yesterday*.

examples.text: I **lost** my phone **last week**.
I**'ve lost** my phone. Can you call it?
**When did** you **buy** that dress?
**Have** you **bought** the tickets?

mistakes.wrong: I've seen that film last night.
mistakes.right: I saw that film last night.
mistakes.why: last night is finished: past simple

mistakes.wrong: When have you got home?
mistakes.right: When did you get home?

mistakes.wrong: I have visited my aunt on Sunday.
mistakes.right: I visited my aunt on Sunday.
mistakes.why: on Sunday is finished: past simple

points.title: Have you ever…? Yes, I went there in…
points.summary: Use the present perfect to **ask about or introduce** an experience, then the past simple for the **details** (when, where, how).

blocks.md: Conversations about experiences often start with the present perfect and continue in the past simple:
*A: **Have** you ever **been** to Isfahan?*
*B: Yes, I **have**. I **went** there last spring.*
*A: Really? What **did** you **think** of it?*
*B: I **loved** it. We **stayed** near the bridge.*
The first question is about life up to now (no time). The follow-up questions are about a **specific** visit, so they use the past simple.
*Have you been…?* asks about the experience. *When did you go?* asks about the details.

examples.text: I**'ve met** a famous actor. I **met** him at the airport in Dubai.
**Have** you **tried** this café? ~ Yes, I **had** lunch there on Monday.
She**'s won** a lot of prizes. She **won** her first one when she was ten.

mistakes.wrong: Have you ever been to Japan? ~ Yes, I've been there in 2018.
mistakes.right: Have you ever been to Japan? ~ Yes, I went there in 2018.
mistakes.why: Details with a time: past simple.

mistakes.wrong: I've seen the match. It has been fantastic.
mistakes.right: I've seen the match. It was fantastic.
mistakes.why: Details about the match: past simple.

points.title: Still true now, or finished?
points.summary: *I**'ve lived** here for ten years* = I still live here. *I **lived** there for ten years* = I don't now. People who are dead: past simple.

blocks.md: With *for* and with situations, the tense tells you if the situation is **still true**:

rows: *He**'s worked** at the bank for five years.* (he still does)
*He **worked** at the bank for five years.* (he doesn't now)

blocks.md: When we talk about people who are **no longer alive**, or periods that are over, we use the past simple: *Hafez **wrote** beautiful poetry.* For living people whose work continues, the present perfect is common: *This author **has written** twelve novels* (and may write more).
Think about **now**: Is the situation still going on? Can the person still do it? If not, use the past simple.

examples.text: My grandfather **lived** in Tabriz all his life.
My parents **have lived** in Tabriz all their lives.
Picasso **painted** thousands of works.
She**'s** already **written** three books, and she's only 25.

mistakes.wrong: I've worked there for three years, but then I left.
mistakes.right: I worked there for three years, but then I left.

mistakes.wrong: Einstein has won the Nobel Prize.
mistakes.right: Einstein won the Nobel Prize.
mistakes.why: He's no longer alive: past simple.

points.title: Today, this morning, this year: finished or not?
points.summary: *this morning, today, this week* take the present perfect if the period **isn't over** and the past simple if it **is over**.

blocks.md: Some time phrases can mean a finished or an unfinished period. It depends on **when you are speaking**:

With ***today, this week, this month, this year***, the present perfect is the usual choice while the period continues: *It**'s been** a busy week.* At the end of a period, people often use the past simple: *(on Friday evening) It **was** a busy week.*
If you mention a specific time **within** the unfinished period, use the past simple: *I**'ve** spoken to her **today**. I **spoke** to her **at 9**.*

examples.text: (at 11 am) I**'ve sent** ten emails this morning.
(at 6 pm) I **sent** ten emails this morning.
I**'ve** seen her **today**. We **had** lunch together **at one**.
We**'ve had** a lot of rain **this year**.

mistakes.wrong: (at 9 pm) Have you seen the doctor this morning?
mistakes.right: (at 9 pm) Did you see the doctor this morning?
mistakes.why: At 9 pm the morning is over.

mistakes.wrong: I've phoned him at 10 o'clock today.
mistakes.right: I phoned him at 10 o'clock today.

points.title: American and British English
points.summary: In American English, the past simple is common with *just, already, yet* and *ever*: *I just ate. Did you finish yet?* British English prefers the present perfect.

blocks.md: Both varieties use the present perfect, but American English often uses the **past simple** where British English uses the present perfect, especially with *just, already, yet, ever* and for recent news:

rows: ***Did** you ever **go** to Mexico?* / ***Have** you ever **been**…?*

blocks.md: Both forms are correct. In exams and international English, the present perfect is the safer choice with these words. With a **finished time** (*yesterday, ago*), both varieties use the past simple.
American English also uses *gotten* as a past participle of *get* in some meanings: *It's **gotten** colder.* British English: *It's **got** colder.*

examples.text: (BrE) *Have you **had** lunch yet?* / (AmE) *Did you **have** lunch yet?*
(BrE) *She**'s just left**.* / (AmE) *She **just left**.*
(both) *She **left** ten minutes ago.*

mistakes.wrong: (in any variety) I've just finished it ten minutes ago.
mistakes.right: I finished it ten minutes ago.
mistakes.why: With ago, only the past simple.

mistakes.wrong: (in any variety) Did you see him yet yesterday?
mistakes.right: Did you see him yesterday?
mistakes.why: yet doesn't go with a finished time.

points.title: When both are possible: the meaning changes
points.summary: Sometimes both tenses are correct, with a different focus: *I've always wanted* (still) vs *I always wanted* (not now); *Have you heard?* vs *Did you hear?*

blocks.md: In some contexts, both tenses are grammatical. The choice shows how the speaker sees the event:

items: *I**'ve always wanted** to visit Japan.* (I still want to.) / *I **always wanted** to visit Japan.* (Maybe I've visited now, or I've given up.)
***Have** you **heard**? They're getting married!* (news, now) / ***Did** you **hear** the news this morning?* (a specific occasion)
*I**'ve recently started** running.* / *I **recently started** running.* (Both are fine with *recently*.)
*Who**'s eaten** my sandwich?* (I've just noticed; the result) / *Who **ate** my sandwich?* (also natural, especially in American English)

blocks.md: Speakers also switch tense to show **distance**: *I **haven't seen** him since the party* (up to now) / *I **didn't see** him at the party* (one occasion).

With ***already, just, yet, ever*** and ***recently***, both tenses are acceptable in modern English, though the present perfect is the standard in British English. With **finished time expressions**, only the past simple is correct.

examples.text: My father **has always loved** gardening.
My father **always loved** gardening.
examples.note: he has probably died, or it's no longer true

examples.text: **Have** you **seen** my glasses? I can't find them.
**Did** you **see** my glasses when you were in the kitchen?

mistakes.wrong: I always wanted to try sushi, and I still want to.
mistakes.right: I've always wanted to try sushi, and I still want to.

mistakes.wrong: Have you heard the president's speech last night?
mistakes.right: Did you hear the president's speech last night?

items.prompt: *I always wanted to be a pilot.* What does this suggest?
options: I still want to be a pilot.
I never wanted to be a pilot.
The wish belongs to the past; it may not be true now.
items.explanation: Past simple: the situation is seen as finished.

items.prompt: Which sentence suggests that the speaker still loves the city?
options: I loved that city when I was young.
I loved that city for years.
I loved this city when I lived here.

items.prompt: I ___ (always / want) to learn the piano, and now I'm finally taking lessons.
items.explanation: Both are possible: *have always wanted* connects the wish to now; *always wanted* sees it as past.

topics.summary: The past connected to now: I've lost my keys. Have you ever been to Rome?
intro: We use the **present perfect** (*have / has* + past participle) to connect the past with **now**: *I**'ve lost** my keys* (I can't find them now). *She**'s been** to Japan three times* (in her life, up to now).

The important thing is not **when** it happened but that it matters **now**. If you say when (*yesterday, in 2020*), use the past simple. See [Present Perfect vs Past Simple](/blog/grammar/present-perfect-vs-past-simple/).

points.title: Form: have / has + past participle
points.summary: **have / has + past participle**: *I've finished. She hasn't called. Have you eaten?*

blocks.md: The **past participle** of regular verbs ends in *-ed*, like the past simple: *work → worked, play → played*. Irregular verbs have their own form:
*He's* can mean *he is* or *he has*. If the next word is a past participle, it's *has*: *He**'s gone*** = he has gone. *He**'s going*** = he is going.

examples.text: We**'ve bought** a new car.
She **hasn't done** her homework.
**Have** you **seen** my phone?
My parents **have** never **eaten** sushi.

mistakes.wrong: She have finished.
mistakes.right: She has finished.

mistakes.wrong: I have went to Spain.
mistakes.right: I have been to Spain.
mistakes.why: Use the past participle (been / gone), not the past simple.

mistakes.wrong: Have you ate breakfast?
mistakes.right: Have you eaten breakfast?

points.title: Experiences: ever, never, before
points.summary: Use the present perfect for **life experiences** up to now, without saying when: *Have you ever been to Canada? I've never tried sushi.*

blocks.md: When we talk about experiences in our life (at any time up to now), we use the present perfect. We don't say **when**:

items: *I**'ve been** to Italy three times.*
***Have** you **ever ridden** a horse?* (ever = at any time in your life)
*She**'s never seen** snow.* (never = at no time)
*I**'ve met** him **before**.*

blocks.md: ***Ever*** is used in questions; ***never*** makes the sentence negative (don't add *not*): *I've **never** been there.* Not *I haven't never been there*.
If you then give details (when, where, how), change to the **past simple**: *I**'ve been** to Rome. I **went** there in 2019 with my family.*
*Been to* = went and came back (an experience). *I've been to Paris* = I visited Paris at some time in my life.

examples.text: **Have** you **ever eaten** Persian food?
I**'ve never flown** in a helicopter.
We**'ve seen** this film before.
How many countries **have** you **visited**?

mistakes.wrong: I have never not been to Asia.
mistakes.right: I have never been to Asia.

mistakes.wrong: Have you ever went to Rome?
mistakes.right: Have you ever been to Rome?

mistakes.wrong: I have been to London in 2019.
mistakes.right: I went to London in 2019.
mistakes.why: With a past time: past simple

points.title: Just, already and yet
points.summary: **just** = a short time ago; **already** = sooner than expected; **yet** = up to now (in questions and negatives, at the end).

rows: before now, maybe sooner than expected
before the participle (or at the end)

blocks.md: ***Yet*** in a question asks whether something we expect has happened. In a negative it means it hasn't happened, but we expect it to: *The bus **hasn't come yet**.*
In American English, the past simple is also common with these words: *I **just ate**. Did you **finish yet**?* In British English, the present perfect is the usual choice. Both are correct.

examples.text: Your taxi**'s just arrived**.
I**'ve already paid** the bill.
**Has** the film **started yet**?
We **haven't decided yet**.

mistakes.wrong: I've finished yet.
mistakes.right: I've already finished.
mistakes.why: yet is for questions and negatives

mistakes.wrong: Have you yet finished?
mistakes.right: Have you finished yet?

mistakes.wrong: I've eaten just.
mistakes.right: I've just eaten.

points.title: Been or gone?
points.summary: *She's **gone** to Paris* = she's there now. *She's **been** to Paris* = she went and came back.

rows: She is at the bank now (or on the way).
She went to the bank and she's back now.
She visited Japan at some time in her life.

blocks.md: Use ***gone*** when the person is **still away**. Use ***been*** when the person **has returned**, and for experiences.
*Where have you been?* = you were away and now you're back. *Where has he gone?* = he isn't here now.

examples.text: My parents **have gone** to Mashhad for a week.
Have you ever **been** to Mashhad?
Where **have** you **been**? I've been waiting for an hour!
Ali isn't here. He**'s gone** home.

mistakes.wrong: I've gone to Rome twice.
mistakes.right: I've been to Rome twice.

mistakes.wrong: Where's Reza? ~ He's been to the gym. (he's still there)
mistakes.right: Where's Reza? ~ He's gone to the gym.

points.title: A past action with a result now, and news
points.summary: The present perfect shows that a past action has a **result now** (*I've lost my keys* = I don't have them) and gives **new information**: *The prime minister has resigned.*

blocks.md: We often use the present perfect when a past action is important because of its **result now**:

items: *I**'ve lost** my keys.* (I can't get in now.)
*Somebody **has broken** the window.* (It's broken now.)
*She**'s had** a haircut.* (Her hair looks different now.)

blocks.md: We also use it to give **news**: *The police **have arrested** a man in connection with the robbery.* When we add details (when, how), we usually switch to the past simple: *He **was arrested** at his home last night.*

Compare: *I**'ve lost** my keys* (I still haven't found them) and *I **lost** my keys yesterday, but I found them later* (finished story). See [Present Perfect vs Past Simple](/blog/grammar/present-perfect-vs-past-simple/).

examples.text: The lift **has broken** down again. We'll have to use the stairs.
I**'ve cut** my finger. It's bleeding.
Scientists **have discovered** a new species of frog.
Prices **have gone** up. Everything is more expensive.

mistakes.wrong: Prices have went up.
mistakes.right: Prices have gone up.

mistakes.wrong: The president has resigned yesterday.
mistakes.right: The president resigned yesterday.

points.title: Today, this week, recently, so far
points.summary: Use the present perfect with periods of time that are **not finished**: *today, this week, this year, recently, lately, so far, up to now.*

blocks.md: When the time period **includes now**, use the present perfect:

items: *I**'ve drunk** three coffees **today**.* (Today isn't finished.)
*We **haven't had** any rain **this month**.*
*She**'s been** very busy **recently / lately**.*
***So far**, 200 people **have signed** the letter.*

blocks.md: Compare: *I**'ve seen** her **this morning*** (it's still morning) and *I **saw** her **this morning*** (it's now afternoon, the morning is finished).
***Recently*** can go with both tenses: *I**'ve recently started** yoga* / *I **recently started** yoga.* ***Lately*** usually goes with the present perfect.

examples.text: I **haven't seen** Ali **this week**.
It**'s rained** a lot **this year**.
Have you **been** to the cinema **lately**?
**Up to now**, we **haven't had** any problems.

mistakes.wrong: I've seen her yesterday.
mistakes.right: I saw her yesterday.

mistakes.wrong: Lately I watched a lot of films.
mistakes.right: Lately I've watched a lot of films.

points.title: It's the first time… and the best… I've ever…
points.summary: After *It's the first / second time* and after a superlative + *ever*, use the present perfect: *It's the first time I've driven. It's the best film I've ever seen.*

blocks.md: When we talk about **now**, we use the present perfect after these patterns:

items: ***It's the first time** I**'ve eaten** sushi.* Not *It's the first time I eat sushi*.
*This is the **third time** he**'s been** late this week.*
*She's the **nicest** person I**'ve ever met**.*
*That was the **most boring** film I**'ve ever seen**.*

blocks.md: For a past situation, use the past perfect: *It **was** the first time I**'d** ever **flown**.* See [Past Perfect](/blog/grammar/past-perfect/#ppf-first-time).
*Ever* is optional with superlatives, but very common: *the best meal I've (ever) had*.

examples.text: **This is the first time** I**'ve visited** Canada.
It's the **second time** you**'ve asked** me that today.
This is the **best** coffee I**'ve ever tasted**.
He's the **funniest** person I**'ve** ever **known**.

mistakes.wrong: It's the first time I see snow.
mistakes.right: It's the first time I've seen snow.

mistakes.wrong: This is the best book I ever read.
mistakes.right: This is the best book I've ever read.

points.title: The present perfect in news and reports
points.summary: News and reports often **introduce** a topic with the present perfect and then give the **details** in the past simple: *A storm has hit the coast. It arrived at 3 am and destroyed…*

blocks.md: In news reports, the first sentence often uses the present perfect to present the event as **new and relevant now**. The following sentences, which give details of time, place and manner, use the **past simple**:
*Firefighters **have rescued** a family of five from a burning building in Tabriz. The fire **started** in the kitchen just after midnight, and the family **escaped** through a window.*

In academic and formal writing, the present perfect introduces **recent research or a general state of knowledge**, and the past simple reports **specific studies**: *Several studies **have shown** a link between sleep and memory. In 2019, a team at Oxford **found** that…*
Headlines often drop *have / has* and use the past participle or the present simple: *Fire **destroys** factory. Missing child **found** safe.*

Once you mention a specific past time, place or event, the past simple usually takes over. Going back to the present perfect is possible to sum up: *So far, the fire **has caused** damage worth millions.*

examples.text: The central bank **has raised** interest rates. The decision **was announced** this morning.
Researchers **have developed** a new test for the disease. They **tested** it on 500 patients.
Rescue teams **have found** two more survivors.

mistakes.wrong: A plane has crashed in the mountains. It has crashed at 6 am.
mistakes.right: A plane has crashed in the mountains. It crashed at 6 am.
mistakes.why: With the time detail: past simple.

mistakes.wrong: Smith has published a famous study in 1998.
mistakes.right: Smith published a famous study in 1998.

points.title: When I've finished…: the present perfect for the future
points.summary: In time clauses about the future, the present perfect shows that one action will be **complete** before another: *I'll call you when I've finished.*

blocks.md: After ***when, after, as soon as, until, once, before*** + a future meaning, we don't use *will*. We use the present simple, or the **present perfect** to stress that the first action will be **finished** first:

items: *I'll call you **when** I**'ve finished** the report.* (first finish, then call)
*You can't leave **until** you**'ve answered** all the questions.*
***Once** you**'ve tried** it, you'll love it.*

blocks.md: Often both tenses are possible with little difference: *I'll call you when I **get** home / when I**'ve got** home.* The present perfect is clearer when the first action takes time and must be completed.
Don't use the present perfect when the two actions happen **at the same time**: *When I **see** her, I'll tell her.* Not *When I've seen her, I'll tell her* (you tell her while you see her).
See [Future Time Clauses](/blog/grammar/future-time-clauses/) for *when, if, as soon as* with the future.

examples.text: **As soon as** I**'ve saved** enough money, I'm going to buy a car.
Don't send the email **until** you**'ve checked** it.
**After** we**'ve eaten**, we'll go for a walk.
**When** I **arrive**, I'll call you.

mistakes.wrong: I'll call you when I will finish.
mistakes.right: I'll call you when I've finished.
mistakes.why: No will in the time clause.

mistakes.wrong: When I've seen him tomorrow, I'll give him the book.
mistakes.right: When I see him tomorrow, I'll give him the book.

items.prompt: *Police ___ a man after a robbery in the city centre. He was arrested at his home on Tuesday.*
items.explanation: The news is introduced with the present perfect; the details follow in the past simple.

items.prompt: In an essay: *A number of researchers ___ this question in recent years.*
items.explanation: A general state of recent research: present perfect.

items.prompt: A strong earthquake has shaken parts of Japan. It ___ (strike) at 4.15 local time.
You can watch TV after you ___ your homework.
items.explanation: Time clause, first action complete: *have done*.

items.prompt: I'll lend you the book when I ___ it.
items.explanation: The reading must be complete first: *have read*.

items.prompt: Once you ___ (fill) in the form, give it to the receptionist.

topics.summary: How to choose: I work (in general) or I'm working (now)?
intro: The **present simple** is for things **in general**: habits, facts and permanent situations. The **present continuous** is for things happening **now or around now**, and for **temporary** situations.
*I **work** from home on Fridays. I**'m working** from home today.*

points.title: Now or in general?
points.summary: Present continuous for now; present simple for habits, facts and things in general.

rows: every day, usually, often, never, on Mondays
now, right now, at the moment, Look!, Listen!

blocks.md: Some verbs (*know, want, like, understand…*) are not normally used in the continuous, even for now: *I **know** the answer* (not *I'm knowing*). See [Stative Verbs](/blog/grammar/stative-verbs/).

examples.text: I usually **walk** to work, but today I**'m taking** the bus.
Water **boils** at 100°C. Look, the water **is boiling**!
**Do** you **play** tennis? – Yes, but I**'m not playing** this week.
Where's Tom? – He**'s having** a shower.
My dad **cooks** on Sundays. He**'s cooking** right now.

mistakes.wrong: Look! The bus comes.
mistakes.right: Look! The bus is coming.

mistakes.wrong: I'm going to the gym every day.
mistakes.right: I go to the gym every day.

mistakes.wrong: She is speaking three languages.
mistakes.right: She speaks three languages.
mistakes.why: A permanent ability, not now: present simple.

points.title: Temporary or permanent?
points.summary: Present continuous for temporary situations; present simple for permanent ones.

rows: *I**'m living** with friends until I find a flat.*
*The river **is flowing** very fast today because of the rain.*

blocks.md: Words like *today, this week, this year, at the moment, until…* often show that a situation is temporary.

examples.text: I **work** in a bank, but this month I**'m working** in our Paris office.
We **live** in Ottawa. We**'re staying** with my aunt in Toronto this week.
Our company **isn't doing** very well this year.
He **teaches** maths, but this term he**'s teaching** physics too.

mistakes.wrong: I stay with my aunt until my flat is ready.
mistakes.right: I'm staying with my aunt until my flat is ready.

mistakes.wrong: My parents are living in the same house all their lives.
mistakes.right: My parents have lived in the same house all their lives.
mistakes.why: From the past until now: present perfect. See Present Perfect.

points.title: Stories, jokes and live commentary
points.summary: In informal stories and live commentary, the present continuous gives the background and the present simple gives the main events.

blocks.md: In **informal stories and jokes**, speakers often use present tenses to make the story more vivid. The **present continuous** gives the background; the **present simple** gives the main events, in order: *So I**'m standing** at the bus stop, and this man **comes** up to me and **asks** for my phone.*
After past tenses, a present simple verb can highlight a sudden event, often with *suddenly* or *all of a sudden*: *We were having dinner when all of a sudden the lights **go** out.*

**Live commentary** (sport, demonstrations) works the same way: present simple for quick, complete actions, present continuous for longer ones: *Silva **passes** to Jones… Jones **shoots**! The fans **are going** wild.*

examples.text: So I**'m waiting** for a taxi when a woman **runs** up to me…
A man **walks** into a café and **orders** a coffee…
It**'s raining**, it**'s getting** dark, and suddenly the car **stops**.
And she **serves**… it's an ace!
The crowd **is cheering** as the runners **cross** the line.

mistakes.wrong: So I'm walking home and suddenly a dog is jumping at me.
mistakes.right: So I'm walking home and suddenly a dog jumps at me.

mistakes.wrong: So I stand at the bus stop, and a man is coming up to me.
mistakes.right: So I'm standing at the bus stop, and a man comes up to me.

items.prompt: In an informal story told in present tenses, which tense usually gives the main events?
items.explanation: Main events: **present simple**; background: present continuous.

items.prompt: So I'm sitting on the train, reading, and suddenly a man ___ next to me.
items.explanation: A main event in the story: present simple, *sits down*.

items.prompt: In live sports commentary, which sentence describes a quick, complete action?

topics.summary: Habits, facts, timetables and more: I work, she works, do you work?
intro: We use the **present simple** for habits, routines and things that are generally true: *I **drink** coffee every morning. The sun **rises** in the east.*
With **he, she, it**, add **-s** to the verb: *She **works** in a bank.* For negatives and questions, use **do / does**: *I **don't** like fish. **Does** he **speak** French?*

points.title: Form: I work, she works
points.summary: Use the base verb with I, you, we, they; add -s or -es with he, she, it.

rows: work → works, read → reads, live → lives
kiss → kisses, wash → washes, watch → watches, fix → fixes, go → goes, do → does
study → studies, try → tries, fly → flies
play → plays, buy → buys, enjoy → enjoys

blocks.md: **Be** is different: *I **am**, you **are**, she **is**.* Don't use *am / is / are* with another verb in the present simple: *I **work*** (not *I am work*).

examples.text: I **live** in a small flat.
My brother **works** in a hospital.
He **watches** football every weekend.
My daughter **studies** in the evening.
She **has** two cats.

mistakes.wrong: She work in a bank.
mistakes.right: She works in a bank.

mistakes.wrong: My mother haves two cars.
mistakes.right: My mother has two cars.

mistakes.wrong: He watchs TV every night.
mistakes.right: He watches TV every night.

mistakes.wrong: I am work every day.
mistakes.right: I work every day.

points.title: Negatives and questions: don't, doesn't, do, does
points.summary: Negatives: don't / doesn't + base verb. Questions: do / does + subject + base verb.

blocks.md: Use **-s** only once. After *doesn't* and *does*, use the base verb: *She doesn't **work**. Does she **work**?* (not *doesn't works*)
Keep the question order: question word + *do / does* + subject + verb: *What **does** this word **mean**?* (not *What means this word?*)

examples.text: We **don't watch** TV in the morning.
She **doesn't eat** meat.
**Do** you **like** coffee? – Yes, I **do**.
**Does** your sister **speak** English?
What time **does** the shop **open**?

mistakes.wrong: He don't like coffee.
mistakes.right: He doesn't like coffee.

mistakes.wrong: She doesn't works on Sundays.
mistakes.right: She doesn't work on Sundays.
mistakes.why: After doesn't, use the base verb.

mistakes.wrong: Does he plays tennis?
mistakes.right: Does he play tennis?
mistakes.why: After does, use the base verb.

mistakes.wrong: Where you live?
mistakes.right: Where do you live?

points.title: Uses: habits, facts and permanent situations
points.summary: Use the present simple for habits, routines, facts, permanent situations and likes.

items: Habits and routines: *I **get up** at 7 o'clock. We **play** football on Saturdays.*
Facts and things that are always true: *Water **boils** at 100°C. The sun **rises** in the east.*
Permanent situations: *My parents **live** in Toronto. She **works** for a big company.*
Likes, dislikes and opinions: *I **love** pizza. He **doesn't like** cold weather.*

blocks.md: Common time words: *every day, every week, on Mondays, in the morning, twice a week.* Ask about frequency with ***How often**…?*: *How often **do** you **go** to the gym?*

*Always, usually, often, sometimes, never* go **before** the main verb but **after** *be*: *I **usually** walk to work. He**'s always** late.* See [Adverbs of Frequency](/blog/grammar/adverbs-of-frequency/).

examples.text: I **get up** at 7 every day.
Water **boils** at 100°C.
My parents **live** in Toronto.
I **love** pizza, but I **don't like** pasta.
How often **do** you **go** to the gym? – Twice a week.

mistakes.wrong: She always is late.
mistakes.right: She is always late.
mistakes.why: Adverbs of frequency go after be.

mistakes.wrong: I go every day to work.
mistakes.right: I go to work every day.
mistakes.why: Time words like every day usually go at the end.

mistakes.wrong: Water is boiling at 100°C.
mistakes.right: Water boils at 100°C.
mistakes.why: For facts that are always true, use the present simple.

points.title: Timetables and schedules: The train leaves at 8
points.summary: Use the present simple for future events on a timetable or schedule.

blocks.md: Use the present simple for **future** events that are on a timetable or a fixed schedule: transport, films, classes, opening times. *The train **leaves** at 8:30 tomorrow. What time **does** the film **start** tonight?*

For **your own plans** with other people, use the present continuous or *be going to*, not the present simple: *I**'m meeting** Sam tonight.* (not *I meet Sam tonight*). See [Future Forms](/blog/grammar/future-forms/).

After *when, as soon as, before, after, until*, use the present simple for the future: *I'll call you when I **get** home.* (not *when I will get*). See [Future Time Clauses](/blog/grammar/future-time-clauses/).

examples.text: The train **leaves** at 8:30 tomorrow.
What time **does** the film **start** tonight?
My English course **starts** on Monday.
The museum **opens** at 10 on Sundays.
I'll text you when the plane **lands**.

mistakes.wrong: I meet my friends tonight. (my plan)
mistakes.right: I'm meeting my friends tonight.

mistakes.wrong: I'll call you when I will get home.
mistakes.right: I'll call you when I get home.
mistakes.why: After when, use the present simple for the future.

points.title: I promise, I agree, I apologise: saying is doing
points.summary: Verbs like promise, agree and apologise do the action when you say them: use the present simple.

blocks.md: Some verbs **perform an action** when you say them. When you say *I promise*, you make a promise. With these verbs, use the present simple, not the continuous: *I **promise** I won't be late.* (not *I'm promising*)
Common verbs: *promise, agree, apologise, suggest, advise, insist, admit, refuse, warn, thank, congratulate, request.*
To sound more polite or formal, add a modal: *I **would suggest** leaving early. I **must insist** that you stay. We **would advise** you to book in advance.*

examples.text: I **promise** I'll call you tomorrow.
I **agree** with you.
I **apologise** for the delay.
I **suggest** we take a taxi.
I **would advise** you to book early.

mistakes.wrong: I'm promising I'll be careful.
mistakes.right: I promise I'll be careful.
mistakes.why: Saying it is the action: present simple.

mistakes.wrong: I'm agree with you.
mistakes.right: I agree with you.
mistakes.why: Agree is a verb: don't add am.

mistakes.wrong: I am apologising for the mistake.
mistakes.right: I apologise for the mistake.
mistakes.why: Saying it is the action: present simple.

points.title: Headlines, summaries, instructions and I hear
points.summary: The present simple is also used in headlines, plot summaries, instructions and to pass on news (I hear, I gather).

items: **Headlines** use the present simple for recent events: *Floods **hit** northern Italy. Minister **resigns**.*
**Summaries** of books, films and plays: *In the film, a young doctor **moves** to a small town and **discovers** a secret.*
**Instructions and demonstrations**: *First you **heat** the oil, then you **add** the onions.*
**Passing on news** with *I hear, I gather, I understand, they say, (someone) tells me*: *I **hear** you're moving to Vancouver. Anna **tells** me you've got a new job.*

blocks.md: In these uses, the present simple doesn't mean *now* or *regularly*. It's a convention that makes the text short and lively. In a summary, stay in the present simple: don't switch to the past in the middle.

examples.text: Scientists **discover** water on Mars.
In chapter 3, the author **compares** the two cities.
First you **mix** the flour and the eggs.
I **gather** the meeting has been cancelled.
My doctor **tells** me I need more exercise.

mistakes.wrong: In the film, the hero moves to London and was finding a job.
mistakes.right: In the film, the hero moves to London and finds a job.
mistakes.why: In a summary, keep the present simple.

mistakes.wrong: Anna is telling me you're engaged.
mistakes.right: Anna tells me you're engaged.
mistakes.why: To pass on news, use tells me.

items.prompt: Which headline is written in the usual headline style?
options: Prime Minister Has Resigned After a Vote
The Prime Minister Is Resigning After Vote
items.explanation: Headlines use the **present simple** for recent events.

items.prompt: What does *I gather the meeting is cancelled* mean?
options: I'm collecting things for the meeting.
I've heard that the meeting is cancelled.
I want the meeting to be cancelled.
items.explanation: *I gather* = I understand from what I've heard or read.

items.prompt: Choose the best sentence for a film summary.
options: The hero moves to London and finds a job in a bank.
The hero has moved to London and has been finding a job.
The hero is moving to London and is finding a job.
The hero moved to London and is finding a job.

topics.h1: Quantifiers: All, Most, Each, Every, None
topics.summary: Words that say how many: all students, most of my friends, every day, each of them, both, neither, none.
intro: **Quantifiers** tell us how many or how much: *all, most, some, none, each, every, both, either, neither*. Many can be used with or without ***of***: *most people / most of the people*.

For *much, many, a few* and *a little*, see [Much, Many, A Few, A Little](/blog/grammar/much-many-a-few-a-little/). For *both… and* and *either… or*, see [Both… And, Either… Or](/blog/grammar/both-either-neither-not-only/).

points.title: All, most, some, no: with or without of
points.summary: Use ***all / most / some / no*** + noun for things **in general** (*Most people like music*). Use ***all of / most of / some of / none of*** + ***the / my / these*** + noun, or a pronoun, for a **specific** group (*Most of my friends live here*).

rows: ***All (of) the** children in my class are friendly.*
***Most of the** people I know work hard.*
***Some of the** shops in my street are closed.*

blocks.md: With a **pronoun**, always use *of*: ***most of them**, **some of us**, **all of it**, **none of you***.
***All*** can drop *of* before *the / my / these*: ***all the** students = **all of the** students*. *Most* and *some* can't: ***most of the** students* (not *most the students*).

examples.text: **Most** people in Canada speak English.
**Most of my** friends are married.
**All of us** were tired.
**None of the** shops were open.

mistakes.wrong: Most of people like chocolate.
mistakes.right: Most people like chocolate.

mistakes.wrong: Most the students passed.
mistakes.right: Most of the students passed.

mistakes.wrong: All of them is here.
mistakes.right: All of them are here.

points.title: Each or every?
points.summary: ***Each*** and ***every*** + **singular** noun + **singular** verb. ***Every*** = all of a group, seen together (*Every student passed*). ***Each*** = one by one, separately (*Each child got a present*). Only ***each*** can be used with ***of*** or alone.

rows: one by one: *Each player has a number.*
all together: *Every player wants to win.*
also for two: *She had a ring on each hand.*

blocks.md: Both take a **singular** verb: ***Every** room **has** a TV. **Each** of the rooms **has** a TV.*
For things that happen regularly, use ***every***: ***every** morning, **every** two weeks* (not *each two weeks*).

examples.text: **Every** child needs love.
The teacher spoke to **each** student individually.
**Each of** my parents has a car.
I go to the gym **every** other day.

mistakes.wrong: Every of the students has a laptop.
mistakes.right: Each of the students has a laptop.

mistakes.wrong: Every students are here.
mistakes.right: Every student is here.

mistakes.wrong: I visit my parents each two weeks.
mistakes.right: I visit my parents every two weeks.

points.title: Both, either, neither (of)
points.summary: For **two** things: ***both*** = the one and the other (+ plural); ***either*** = one or the other (+ singular); ***neither*** = not one and not the other (+ singular). With ***of***: *both of / either of / neither of* + ***the / my / them***.

rows: *both of the children, both of them*
*either of the days, either of them*
*neither of the answers, neither of them*

blocks.md: ***Neither*** is already negative, so use a **positive** verb: ***Neither** of them **came**.* (not *didn't come*). In negative sentences, use ***either***: *I **don't** like **either** of them.*
After ***neither of / either of***, a **singular** verb is more formal and a plural verb is common in speech: *Neither of my parents **speaks / speak** English.*
For **more than two**, use *all, any* and *none*: *None of my three brothers…*

examples.text: **Both** my brothers live in Toronto.
You can park on **either** side of the street.
**Neither** restaurant was open.
I don't like **either** of these shirts.

mistakes.wrong: Both of them is teachers.
mistakes.right: Both of them are teachers.

mistakes.wrong: Neither of them didn't come.
mistakes.right: Neither of them came.

mistakes.wrong: I don't want neither of them.
mistakes.right: I don't want either of them.

points.title: All or whole? All, everything, no and none
points.summary: ***The whole*** + singular noun = all of one thing (*the whole day, the whole cake*). ***All*** goes with uncountable and plural nouns (*all the money, all the people*). ***Everything*** is more natural than *all* alone. ***None*** stands alone; ***no*** needs a noun.

rows: *I spent **the whole** day at home. She ate **the whole** pizza.*
***Everything** is fine.* (*All is fine* sounds old-fashioned)
***All** I want is some rest.* (= the only thing)

blocks.md: ***All day / all night / all week*** (no *the*) = the whole day: *I worked **all day**.*
***All*** goes **before** the main verb but **after** *be* and auxiliaries: *We **all** love it. We're **all** tired. They've **all** gone.*

examples.text: I read **the whole** book in one night.
**All** my friends came.
**Everything** went well.
**All** we need is a little more time.
How many tickets are left? ~ **None**.

mistakes.wrong: She spent whole day shopping.
mistakes.right: She spent the whole day shopping.

mistakes.wrong: There are none tickets.
mistakes.right: There are no tickets.

points.title: None of them is or are? All of whom, each and every
points.summary: ***None of*** + plural takes a **singular** verb in formal style and a **plural** verb in everyday English. In relative clauses, use ***all / most / none / both of whom / which***. ***Each and every*** is emphatic. ***Not all*** ≠ ***none***.

rows: ***None of** the candidates **was / were** suitable.* (singular = formal)
*She has three sons, **all of whom** are doctors. I bought two books, **neither of which** was cheap.*
***Each and every** one of you has helped.*
***Not all** students passed.* (some failed) / ***None** of the students passed.*
*every other day* (= every second day), *every few weeks*
***all of us*** (not *all us*); *us all* after a verb: *She thanked **us all**.*

blocks.md: *All… not* can be ambiguous: *All the students didn't pass* may mean *not all*. Write ***Not all** the students passed* or ***None** of the students passed* to be clear.
After a comma, *all of them / both of them* + verb starts a new clause, so it needs *and* or a full stop. In one sentence, use ***of whom / of which***.

examples.text: **None of** the reports **has** been published yet.
I have two brothers, **both of whom** live abroad.
**Not all** doctors agree with this.
I see my parents **every other** weekend.

mistakes.wrong: I have three sisters, all of them are married.
mistakes.right: I have three sisters, all of whom are married.

mistakes.wrong: All us were tired.
mistakes.right: All of us were tired.

items.prompt: He has three daughters, ___ are lawyers.
Which sentence means that some students passed and some failed?
I go to the gym every ___ day: Monday, Wednesday, Friday… (one word)

topics.h1: Question Tags (…, isn't it? …, don't you?)
topics.summary: Short questions at the end of a sentence to check or ask for agreement: It's cold, isn't it? You like coffee, don't you?
intro: A **question tag** is a short question at the end of a sentence: *It's a nice day, **isn't it**?* We use tags to **check** information or to ask the listener to **agree**.
Usually, a **positive** sentence has a **negative** tag, and a **negative** sentence has a **positive** tag. The tag uses the same auxiliary as the sentence.

points.title: Positive sentence, negative tag (and the other way)
points.summary: Positive + negative tag: *You're Iranian, **aren't you**?* Negative + positive tag: *She doesn't eat meat, **does she**?* Use the same auxiliary as the sentence.

blocks.md: Use the **auxiliary** from the sentence (*be, have, can, will…*). If there's no auxiliary, use ***do / does / did***.
The tag uses a **pronoun**, not a name: *Ali works here, doesn't **he**?* (not *doesn't Ali*)

examples.text: It's hot today, **isn't it**?
You like football, **don't you**?
Your sister lives in Rome, **doesn't she**?
They didn't call, **did they**?

mistakes.wrong: You're tired, isn't it?
mistakes.right: You're tired, aren't you?
mistakes.why: same verb and subject: aren't you

mistakes.wrong: She went home, wasn't she?
mistakes.right: She went home, didn't she?

mistakes.wrong: Tom is here, isn't Tom?
mistakes.right: Tom is here, isn't he?

points.title: Intonation: a real question or asking for agreement?
points.summary: **Rising** intonation (↗) = a real question, I'm not sure. **Falling** intonation (↘) = I'm sure, I want you to agree.

blocks.md: The meaning of a tag depends on your voice:

items: **Rising** (↗): you don't know the answer and really ask: *You're coming tonight, aren't you? ↗* (I'm not sure.)
**Falling** (↘): you're fairly sure and want the listener to agree: *It's a lovely day, isn't it? ↘* (I'm sure it is.)

blocks.md: Tags with falling intonation are very common in small talk, about the weather, food, or shared experiences.

examples.text: It's really cold, isn't it? ↘
You've got the tickets, haven't you? ↗
That was a fantastic film, wasn't it? ↘
The meeting's at three, isn't it? ↗

mistakes.wrong: It's a lovely day, is it? (asking for agreement)
mistakes.right: It's a lovely day, isn't it?

points.title: Special tags: aren't I, let's… shall we, imperatives, there is
points.summary: **I am → aren't I?** **Let's → shall we?** Imperatives → **will you? / won't you? / can you?** **There is → isn't there?** **Everybody → they**.

blocks.md: After ***everyone, everybody, someone, nobody***, the tag uses ***they***: *Somebody called, didn't **they**?* After ***everything, nothing***, use ***it***: *Everything's ready, isn't **it**?*

examples.text: I'm right, **aren't I**?
Let's have a break, **shall we**?
Pass me the salt, **would you**?
There's no milk, **is there**?
examples.note: there is + negative word → is there

mistakes.wrong: I'm late, amn't I?
mistakes.right: I'm late, aren't I?

mistakes.wrong: Let's go, don't we?
mistakes.right: Let's go, shall we?

mistakes.wrong: Nobody came, did he?
mistakes.right: Nobody came, did they?

points.title: Never, hardly, no one: negative words take a positive tag
points.summary: Sentences with **never, hardly, rarely, no, nobody, nothing** are negative, so the tag is **positive**: *You never call me, **do you**?*

blocks.md: Words like ***never, seldom, rarely, hardly, scarcely, no, nobody, nothing, nowhere*** make the sentence **negative**, even without *not*. So use a **positive** tag: *She hardly eats anything, **does she**?*
Remember the pronoun rules: *Nobody knows, do **they**? Nothing happened, did **it**?*

examples.text: You **never** listen to me, **do you**?
He **hardly** ever smiles, **does he**?
**No one** was hurt, **were they**?
There's **nothing** we can do, **is there**?

mistakes.wrong: You never call me, don't you?
mistakes.right: You never call me, do you?

mistakes.wrong: Nobody saw it, didn't they?
mistakes.right: Nobody saw it, did they?

points.title: Same-way tags and tags in requests
points.summary: **Positive + positive** tags show surprise, interest or irony: *So you're the new boss, **are you**?* Negative sentence + positive tag in polite requests: *You couldn't help me, **could you**?*

blocks.md: **Same-way tags** (positive sentence + positive tag) don't really ask for information. They show **surprise, interest, or sarcasm**, and they often follow *so* or *oh*: *Oh, you're a chef, **are you**? So you think it's funny, **do you**?*
In polite **requests**, a negative statement with a positive tag sounds tentative and polite: *You **couldn't** lend me £10, **could you**? You **wouldn't** have a pen, **would you**?*
***I don't suppose … , do you / could you?*** is another tentative pattern: *I don't suppose you know where she is, **do you**?*
Same-way tags with an angry tone can sound aggressive: *Oh, you want a fight, do you?* Use them carefully.

examples.text: So you've finally arrived, **have you**?
You're moving to Japan, **are you**? How exciting!
You couldn't open the window, **could you**?
I don't suppose you've seen my keys, **have you**?

mistakes.wrong: You couldn't help me, couldn't you?
mistakes.right: You couldn't help me, could you?

items.prompt: Which sentence shows surprise or interest?
options: You aren't a doctor, are you?
Oh, you're a doctor, are you?
items.explanation: Positive + positive tag = surprise or interest.

items.prompt: Which is the most polite request?
options: You can give me a lift, can't you?
You couldn't give me a lift, could you?
Will you give me a lift?
items.explanation: Negative sentence + positive tag sounds tentative and polite.

items.prompt: I don't suppose you know the answer, ___? (two words)

topics.summary: How to make questions: Are you…? Do you…? Where do you live? Who called you? What is it like? Don't you like it?
intro: In English questions, the **auxiliary verb** (*be, do, have, can, will…*) usually comes **before** the subject: ***Are** you hungry? **Do** you like tea? **Can** she swim?*

With question words (*what, where, when…*), the word goes first: ***Where do** you live?* This page goes from basic questions to negative and echo questions. For *Do you know where…?*, see [Indirect Questions](/blog/grammar/indirect-questions/).

points.title: Yes/no questions: Are you…? Do you…? Can you…?
points.summary: Put **be** or an **auxiliary** (*do, does, did, can, will, have*) before the subject: *Are you ready? Does she work here? Can you swim?*

blocks.md: With *be* and modals, just change the order. With other verbs, add ***do / does / did*** and use the **base verb**: ***Does** she **like** it?* Not *Does she likes it?*
Short answers repeat the auxiliary: *Yes, she **does**. / No, I **can't**. / Yes, they **are**.*

examples.text: **Are** you a student? ~ Yes, I **am**.
**Do** you speak English? ~ Yes, I **do**.
**Did** they win the match? ~ No, they **didn't**.
**Have** you finished? ~ Not yet.

mistakes.wrong: You are hungry? (in writing)
mistakes.right: Are you hungry?

mistakes.wrong: Does she likes coffee?
mistakes.right: Does she like coffee?

mistakes.wrong: Do you can swim?
mistakes.right: Can you swim?

points.title: Wh- question words: what, where, when, who, why, how
points.summary: Put the question word **first**, then the auxiliary and the subject: *Where do you live? What is your name? Why did she leave?*

blocks.md: Order: **question word + auxiliary / be + subject + main verb**: ***Where do** you **work**?* ***What are** you **doing**?*

examples.text: **What** is your phone number?
**Where** did you go on holiday?
**Why** is the shop closed?
**Whose** keys are these?

mistakes.wrong: Where you live?
mistakes.right: Where do you live?

mistakes.wrong: What time the film starts?
mistakes.right: What time does the film start?

mistakes.wrong: Why you are sad?
mistakes.right: Why are you sad?

points.title: How much, how many, how long, how often, how far
points.summary: **How + adjective / adverb** asks about amount, time and frequency: *How much is it? How long does it take? How often do you exercise?*

blocks.md: ***How long does it take** (to…)?* asks about the time a journey or job needs: *How long does it take to get to the airport? ~ It takes about 40 minutes.*
***How much*** goes with uncountable nouns (*money, time, water*); ***how many*** with plural nouns (*people, books*).

examples.text: **How much** does this jacket cost?
**How many** brothers and sisters do you have?
**How long** does it take to walk there?
**How often** do you visit your parents?

mistakes.wrong: How many money do you have?
mistakes.right: How much money do you have?

mistakes.wrong: How long it takes to get there?
mistakes.right: How long does it take to get there?

points.title: Who saw you? or Who did you see? Subject and object questions
points.summary: When **who / what** is the **subject**, don't use *do / did*: *Who called you?* When it's the **object**, use *do / did*: *Who did you call?*

blocks.md: Ask yourself: is the question word the person or thing that **does** the action? If yes, it's the **subject**: use normal word order, no *do*: ***Who broke** the window? ~ Tom did.*
If the question word is the person or thing that **receives** the action, use *do / does / did*: ***Who did** Tom **see**? ~ He saw Maria.*

examples.text: **Who told** you that?
**Who did** you **tell**?
**What happened** at the meeting?
**Which team won** the match?

mistakes.wrong: What did happen?
mistakes.right: What happened?

mistakes.wrong: Who did break the window? (asking who did it)
mistakes.right: Who broke the window?

mistakes.wrong: Who you saw at the party?
mistakes.right: Who did you see at the party?

points.title: Who is she talking to? What is it like? Prepositions at the end
points.summary: In questions, prepositions usually go at the **end**: *Who are you talking **to**? Where are you **from**?* **What is it like?** = describe it.

blocks.md: When a verb has a preposition (*talk to, look at, come from, wait for, think about*), the preposition goes at the **end** of the question: *What are you looking **at**? Who is this present **for**?*
***What is … like?*** asks for a **description**: *What's your new school **like**? ~ It's big and modern.* It's different from *Do you like…?* (Do you enjoy it?)
In very formal English, the preposition can go first: ***To whom** did you speak?* In normal English, *Who did you speak to?* is much more common.

examples.text: **Where** are you **from**?
**What** are you thinking **about**?
**Who** is the letter **from**?
**What's** the weather **like** in Vancouver?

mistakes.wrong: From where are you?
mistakes.right: Where are you from?

mistakes.wrong: How is your new boss like?
mistakes.right: What is your new boss like?

points.title: What or which? What kind of…?
points.summary: **which** = a choice from a small, known group: *Which colour do you want, red or blue?* **what** = an open choice: *What colour is your car?*

blocks.md: Use ***which*** when there is a **limited** number of options, often mentioned or obvious: ***Which** of these bags is yours? **Which** way is the station, left or right?*
Use ***what*** for an **open** question with many possible answers: ***What** music do you like? **What** time is it?*
***Which one(s)?*** and ***which of*** + plural: ***Which one** do you want? **Which of** your friends is coming?* (Not *what of*.)
***What kind of / what sort of*** asks about a type: ***What kind of** films do you like?*

examples.text: **Which** do you prefer, tea or coffee?
**What** do you want for your birthday?
**Which of** these photos do you like best?
**What kind of** job are you looking for?

mistakes.wrong: What of these is yours?
mistakes.right: Which of these is yours?

mistakes.wrong: What one do you want?
mistakes.right: Which one do you want?

points.title: Negative questions: Don't you…? Isn't it…?
points.summary: Negative questions (*Don't you…? Isn't it…? Haven't you…?*) show **surprise**, ask for **agreement**, or check something we **expect** to be true.

blocks.md: Negative questions are used:

items: for **surprise**: ***Don't** you **like** chocolate?* (I'm surprised.)
to ask for **agreement**: ***Isn't** it a beautiful day?* (I think it is.)
to check what we **expect**: ***Haven't** we **met** before?* (I think we have.)
in **complaints**: ***Can't** you be quiet?*

blocks.md: Answering: answer about the **fact**, not the question form: *Don't you like coffee? ~ **No**, I don't. (= I don't like it) / **Yes**, I do. (= I like it)*
In formal English, *not* can go after the subject: ***Do you not** agree?*

examples.text: **Don't** you **remember** me?
**Isn't** this view amazing?
**Haven't** you **finished** yet?
**Wouldn't** it be better to wait?

mistakes.wrong: Don't you like it? ~ No, I like it.
mistakes.right: Don't you like it? ~ Yes, I do. / Yes, I like it.

mistakes.wrong: Do you don't want it?
mistakes.right: Don't you want it?

points.title: Echo questions and statement questions: You did what?
points.summary: **Echo questions** repeat part of what someone said to show surprise or check: *She's moving to Peru. ~ She's moving where?* **Statement questions** keep normal word order with rising intonation: *You're leaving?*

blocks.md: An **echo question** repeats the sentence and replaces the surprising part with a question word, with strong stress: *I paid $500 for it. ~ You paid **how much**?* *He married his boss. ~ He married **who**?*

A **statement question** uses normal word order with **rising** intonation. It checks or expresses surprise about something we think we heard or understood: *You've finished **already**?* *So you're not coming?*
Short **reply questions** show interest: *I've just got engaged. ~ **Have you**? Congratulations!* See [So Do I, Neither Do I](/blog/grammar/so-do-i-neither-do-i/).
These are spoken forms. In writing, use normal questions, except in dialogue.

examples.text: I've sold the car. ~ You've sold **what**?
They're getting married in Bali. ~ **Where**?
You're not hungry? I made a huge dinner!
He's 90. ~ **Is he**? He looks much younger.

mistakes.wrong: You paid how much? (in a formal essay)
mistakes.right: How much did you pay?

items.prompt: *I've eaten twelve pancakes.* ~ *You've eaten ___?*
items.explanation: Echo question: replace the number with *how many*.

items.prompt: Which is a statement question?
*Ali has bought a horse.* ~ *He's bought a ___?* (one word)

topics.summary: Words that make adjectives weaker or stronger: a bit cold, fairly good, quite nice, pretty busy, rather expensive.
intro: ***Fairly, quite, pretty*** and ***rather*** go before adjectives and adverbs to mean “more than a little, but not very”: *The test was **fairly** easy. It's **pretty** cold today.*
Their exact meaning depends on the word after them, on your voice, and on British or American English.

points.title: A bit, fairly, quite, very: how strong?
points.summary: From weaker to stronger: ***a bit / a little*** < ***fairly*** < ***quite / pretty*** < ***very / really*** < ***extremely***.

rows: more than a little, not very
a bit more than *fairly* (*pretty* is informal)

blocks.md: ***A bit*** is common with **negative** adjectives: *It's **a bit** expensive. I'm **a bit** tired.*
These words come **before** the adjective: *It's **quite** big.* With a noun, the usual order is ***quite a*** + adjective + noun: *It's **quite a** big house.*

examples.text: I'm **a bit** hungry.
My English is **fairly** good.
The restaurant was **pretty** busy.
She's **really** kind.

mistakes.wrong: It's very much cold.
mistakes.right: It's very cold.

mistakes.wrong: I'm a few tired.
mistakes.right: I'm a bit tired.

points.title: Quite: fairly or completely?
points.summary: With most adjectives, ***quite*** = **fairly** (*quite good*). With **extreme** or **absolute** adjectives (*amazing, impossible, sure, right*), ***quite*** = **completely** (*quite impossible, quite right*). ***Quite a lot / quite a few*** = a fairly large amount.

rows: I like it, but not very much

blocks.md: In **American English**, *quite* often means *very*: *The food was **quite** good* (= very good). In British English, it often means *fairly*.
***Not quite*** = almost: *I haven't **quite** finished.*

examples.text: The hotel was **quite** nice.
Are you **quite** sure?
I've read **quite a lot of** his books.
I'm **not quite** ready. Give me two minutes.

mistakes.wrong: I quite am sure.
mistakes.right: I'm quite sure.

mistakes.wrong: There were quite much people.
mistakes.right: There were quite a lot of people.

points.title: Rather and pretty: rather expensive, pretty good
points.summary: ***Rather*** is like *quite*, but it often sounds **negative** or **surprised**: *It's rather expensive.* With positive words, it means *surprisingly*: *The film was rather good.* ***Pretty*** is informal: *pretty good, pretty tired*.

rows: *It was **rather a** long day.* = *a **rather** long day*

blocks.md: ***Rather*** is more common in British English and in writing. In everyday American English, *pretty* is more common.
Don't confuse *rather* (= fairly) with ***would rather*** (= prefer): *I'd rather stay at home.*

examples.text: The instructions were **rather** confusing.
I **rather** liked the film.
It was **rather a** strange evening.
I'm **pretty** sure he'll come.

mistakes.wrong: It was a rather good.
mistakes.right: It was rather good.

mistakes.wrong: The test was rather more easy.
mistakes.right: The test was rather easier.

points.title: Somewhat, relatively, reasonably: formal alternatives
points.summary: In formal English, use ***somewhat, slightly, reasonably, moderately*** and ***relatively*** instead of *a bit, quite* or *pretty*: *The results were **somewhat** disappointing. Prices are **relatively** low.* ***Rather*** and ***quite*** can also go with verbs: *I **rather** like it. I **quite** understand.*

blocks.md: ***I quite understand*** = I understand completely (polite). ***I quite like it*** (BrE) = I like it, but not very much.
***Somewhat*** and ***relatively*** are common in academic writing: *These results are **relatively** reliable.*

examples.text: The new system is **somewhat** slower.
Housing is **relatively** cheap in this region.
The restaurant is **reasonably** priced.
I **quite** understand your concern.

mistakes.wrong: The results were somewhat of disappointing.
mistakes.right: The results were somewhat disappointing.

mistakes.wrong: It's relatively a cheap area.
mistakes.right: It's a relatively cheap area.

items.prompt: The results were ___ disappointing, but not a disaster.
Don't worry about the delay. I ___ understand.
The hotel was ___ priced, so we stayed an extra night. (one word)

topics.summary: Myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves, and each other.
intro: Use a **reflexive pronoun** when the subject and the object are the **same** person: *I cut **myself**. She taught **herself** English.*
Use ***each other*** when two or more people do something **to one another**: *They love **each other**.*

points.title: Myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, themselves
points.summary: Use a **reflexive pronoun** when the **subject and object are the same**: *I hurt **myself**. They enjoyed **themselves**.*

blocks.md: Compare: *She looked at **her**.* (another woman) / *She looked at **herself**.* (in the mirror)
Spelling: singular *-self*, plural *-selves*. Say *himself* and *themselves* (not *hisself, theirselves*).

examples.text: I cut **myself** while I was cooking.
Be careful! Don't hurt **yourself**.
The cat is washing **itself**.
We introduced **ourselves** to the new neighbours.
She taught **herself** to play the guitar.

mistakes.wrong: He hurt hisself.
mistakes.right: He hurt himself.

mistakes.wrong: They enjoyed theirselves.
mistakes.right: They enjoyed themselves.

mistakes.wrong: We looked at ourself in the mirror.
mistakes.right: We looked at ourselves in the mirror.

points.title: Enjoy yourself, help yourself, by myself; relax, feel, meet
points.summary: Some verbs often take a reflexive pronoun: ***enjoy yourself, help yourself, behave yourself, introduce yourself***. Many verbs usually **don't** in English: *relax, feel, concentrate, meet, wash, get dressed*. ***By myself*** = alone.

blocks.md: ***Enjoy*** needs an object: *Did you **enjoy yourself**? Did you **enjoy the party**?* (not *Did you enjoy?*)
Use *wash, shave* and *get dressed* without *myself* unless you want to emphasise it: *I got up, **washed** and **got dressed**.*

examples.text: Enjoy **yourselves**!
Please **help yourself** to coffee.
I **feel** much better today.
She lives **by herself**.

mistakes.wrong: Relax yourself and sit down.
mistakes.right: Relax and sit down.

mistakes.wrong: I feel myself tired.
mistakes.right: I feel tired.

mistakes.wrong: We met ourselves at university.
